activities.anchor: The definition deserves unpacking because each clause kills a misconception
activities.caption: pair each clause with the work it does
activities.name: mktClauseMatch

config.prompt: "Creating, presenting and delivering value" — pair each clause with its consequence:

pairs.right: begins before the product exists, in choosing which needs to serve — the discipline is upstream of engineering
the same value poorly communicated is worth less — perception is part of the product, not a spin on it
value that never reaches the customer conveniently is not delivered — distribution is marketing
the firm must keep enough of what it creates to survive — marketing arrives holding hands with finance

config.why: A company that creates value but captures none is a charity; one that captures without creating is in trouble the moment competition arrives.

activities.anchor: Walk it through step by step
activities.caption: bet on where the exchange lands
activities.name: mktGapPredict

config.q: Your offer's net value is +17 — positive. A rival delivers +25 to the same customer. The exchange…
choices: happens anyway — positive is all the equation requires
goes to the rival — value is judged against alternatives
config.why: Value must be positive AND larger than any alternative's — a +17 gap is only attractive if the rival offer isn't +25. Positioning is always relative.

activities.anchor: Three features of the equation repay attention
activities.caption: walk the status-quo test
activities.name: mktStatusBranch

config.root: Every innovation's true rival is quieter than any competitor: doing nothing.

start.text: Your innovation's benefits are real, but the customer can "do nothing" for free. What must be true for the exchange to happen?

choices.label: Net value must beat the status quo's — which has no cost and no risk
Being better than the old product is enough

beat.text: "Do nothing" has benefits (no cost, no risk) and every innovation must beat it — the customer compares offers on net value.

choices.label: Now: why does the same offer carry different values to different people?

better.text: Better than the old product is not the bar — the comparison is net value against the best alternative, and the status quo is always on the menu.

choices.label: Re-run the test, then ask why values differ

segment.text: Different customers weight the terms differently: the commuter weighs time (effort), the student weighs price, the enterprise buyer weighs risk — so a firm aims itself at the segment where its gap is largest.

config.why: A benefit the customer doesn't notice is worth zero — making a real benefit visible raises B as surely as improving the product does.

activities.anchor: Company analysis is the C of the three
activities.caption: file each strength by the VRIO verdict
activities.name: mktVrioBuckets

config.prompt: The VRIO test — Valuable, Rare, hard to Imitate, Organised. File each strength:

items.label: a logistics network built over decades
an advantage that compounds with use
assets listed on a hiring site's job ad

config.why: A strength that passes all four is a durable advantage; one that fails is a feature — company analysis exists to force that honesty before the strategy is written.

activities.anchor: The competitor audit therefore asks three questions
activities.caption: drag the divider — spec sheet versus value gap
activities.name: mktAuditCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to read a rival — drag the divider:

before.label: The feature list
before.text: Their spec sheets, side by side — an offer can improve every year and still lose share, because a competitor's offer improved faster.

after.label: The value gap per segment
after.text: What value they deliver, segment by segment — plotted on the positioning map until the empty space appears: the segment nobody serves well, the strategic prize.

config.why: The indirect half is where audits fail: the cinema competes with every streaming subscription, the city hotel with the videoconference.

activities.caption: find the line Porter would correct
activities.name: mktMiddleSpot

config.prompt: One line of this strategy memo is wrong — click it:
lines: Our plan is to be the cheapest, the most premium, and the broadest, all at once.
The generic strategies have different cost structures.
Broad cost leadership, focused differentiation and niche specialisation are the classic choices.
A firm that tries to be best-at-everything usually achieves lowest-at-something.
Porter named the strategic sin "stuck in the middle" — not choosing.
config.correction: Competing means choosing: the cost structures of the generic strategies cannot all be optimised at once.
config.why: A firm that tries to be best at everything its customers want ends up lowest at something — the sin is not choosing.

config.text: Net value (benefits − price − switching cost) must exceed the customer's best %%0%% or no exchange happens; the value ratio (benefits per unit of total cost) shows why "expensive but excellent" can beat "cheap but mediocre" — a ratio of 4× can coexist with a small absolute margin.
config.hint: What the customer measures your offer against — and the status quo is one of them.

activities.anchor: A worked miniature ties the pieces together
activities.caption: rebuild the coffee-shop analysis in order
activities.name: mktCoffeeOrder

config.prompt: Two campus coffee shops sell identical beans. Rebuild the analysis behind the second one:
items: Company analysis: small space, good atmosphere, no economies of scale — the price war is unwinnable
Customer analysis: students time-poor between lectures, space-hungry during study hours
Competitor audit: the chains — cheaper, faster lines, worse seating
The position follows almost mechanically: speed and a study-friendly room for the between-lectures segment
config.why: Analysis first, position second, tactics third — every tactic traceable back to a number in the value equation.
